## Method

All participants were recruited through Prolific. Responses were excluded if incomplete, flagged by Qualtrics as likely fraudulent, with duplicated Prolific IDs, or failed attention checks. Two pilot studies are reported in the [Pilot Studies](#sec-supp-pilot-studies) section of the Supplementary Materials. The two pre-registered studies used stratified sampling to ensure balanced representation across sex, age, ethnicity (based on simplified U.S. census categories), and political affiliation. (See @tbl-participants in the Supplementary Materials). 

Study 1 (*N*=`r nrow(Study1)`; [pre-registered](https://aspredicted.org/mv2z-t7dw.pdf); data collected `r Study1_date`) and Study 2 (*N*=`r nrow(Study2)`; [pre-registered](https://aspredicted.org/z378hg.pdf); data collected `r Study2_date`) provided the primary empirical test and formal replication/extension, respectively. All data are publicly accessible on the [Open Science Framework](https://osf.io/qfv9d). Detailed discrepancies between the pre-registrations and the reported analyses are documented in @tbl-pre-reg-deviations in the Supplementary Materials. Target sample sizes were determined by a priori power analyses detailed in the pre-registration documents. Post-hoc power analyses are detailed in the result section. 

All participants completed the study on Qualtrics. After providing informed consent, they answered a series of questionnaires presented primarily in randomized order to reduce order effects. Demographic questions were administered at the end of the survey.

Both pre-registered studies aimed to test whether religiosity is positively associated with propensity to seek moral advice from AI chatbots. Religiosity was assessed as self-reported and as a behavioral index. Both studies used the same independent variables (self-reported religiosity and behavioral frequency index), and outcomes (frequency of and interest in seeking moral advice from AI chatbots, respectively) but examined different candidate mediators. We report results of *frequency of seeking moral advice from AI chatbots* in the main body and those of *interest in seeking moral advice from AI chatbots* in the Supplementary Materials, as the patterns of results for interest largely mirrored those for frequency. 

To assess participants' broader disposition to moral consultation, both studies computed composite scores averaging participants' self-reported frequency of and interest in seeking moral advice across 13 non-AI, non-religious sources.

Following the theoretical framework outlined in the Introduction, candidate mediators were organized into six clusters: (a) moral consultation disposition (overall frequency of and interest in seeking moral advice from non-AI, non-religious sources); (b) epistemic humility (open-mindedness on moral issues [@hartman2022], and in Study 1 only, general open-mindedness [@kashdan2009] and intellectual humility assessed via two convergent scales [@alfano2017; @krumrei-mancuso2016]); (c) moral objectivism (*belief in moral objectivity*); (d) positive perception of AI chatbots (perceived authority of AI chatbots as moral advisors, and in Study 1 only, perceived valence of AI chatbots as moral advisors); (e) tendency to anthropomorphize AI chatbots (assessed via the adapted Anthropomorphism Subscale of Godspeed Questionnaire [@bartneck2009]); and (f) other personality traits (fear of negative judgment [@leary1983], self-reflective tendency [@grant2002], and deference to authority using the subscales of Moral Foundations Questionnaire [MFQ-2; @atari2023] and Morality-as-Cooperation Questionnaire [MAC-Q; @curry2019]). Study 1 tested clusters (a)–(d). Study 2 added clusters (e)–(f). @tbl-methods in the Supplementary Materials summarizes all variables used across the two pre-registered studies.
